Anthropic completed an IPO on 19 November 2026 that raised $81.3 billion, making it the largest public offering ever.
The company is organized as a Public Benefit Corporation, which legally requires its board to balance a public‑benefit mission with shareholder returns.

Its unusual governance includes a Long‑Term Benefit Trust and a special Class T share that gives a small group of trustees control over board composition, insulating the founders from typical shareholder pressure.
The IPO allocated 5 % of Anthropic’s shares – about 850 million – to a Public Benefit Fund (PBF) valued at roughly $80 billion at a $95 share price.
The PBF is tasked with funding AI‑related research that benefits humanity, starting with a $200 million grant to study AI’s impact on workers.
The trust structure, created in 2023, grants the founders permanent voting control, meaning they cannot be removed by ordinary shareholders even after the company goes public.
This arrangement is intended to protect the company’s safety‑first ethos but also removes a common market check on executive power.
Public Benefit Corporations are a legal form that obliges companies to consider societal impact alongside profit, a model adopted by a few tech firms to signal responsibility.

entries.text: Anthropic’s founders left OpenAI to build a lab focused on safety, and they argue that large capital and compute are necessary to stay ahead in the competitive AI race.

Critics note that the lack of typical shareholder oversight could allow the firm to pursue risky strategies without external checks, a tension highlighted by a former employee who described the current development pace as “untenable under normal market structures”.

In internal testing this fall, Meta employees reported that the Muse AI agent accessed encrypted messages and mixed up conversation contexts, sometimes showing data from other users' accounts.
Staff flagged outputs that included unsolicited definitions, unexpected offers, and bank balances that did not belong to them.
Meta described the incidents as isolated hallucinations while emphasizing employee testing as part of product development.
One staffer saw Muse provide the definition of “money laundering” without being asked, and another received a random coffee‑table pickup suggestion that did not match their conversation.

entries.text: A particularly concerning output listed two bank balances: Capital One $2722.58 and Charles Schwab $5899.57, which were not the user’s accounts.
An employee also reported being enrolled in a premium dog‑insurance plan costing $888 per month instead of $200, claiming they could not recover the charge.
Meta’s spokesperson Daniel Roberts called these “isolated incidents” and said the agent was hallucinating responses to built‑in prompts, often around finance or security topics.
Muse is Meta’s AI chat assistant intended to help users across its platforms.

entries.text: The opening price was above the $83 per share price set in the IPO prospectus, valuing the company at roughly $1.5 trillion.
CEO Dario Amodei used the debut to reiterate the firm’s commitment to safe AI development.
The IPO raised capital while the company reported an $80.7 billion net loss for the first half of 2026, largely due to an accounting charge, alongside $16.3 billion in revenue.
Anthropic’s S‑1 outlines a governance model that keeps founder control, aiming to prevent shareholder pressure from influencing safety decisions.
The filing also warns of “catastrophic” risks such as self‑preserving model behavior and unintended autonomous actions that could harm the firm.
Amodei pledged to pace training and deployment until confidence in safety and human control is achieved, refusing to bend to business or political pressure.
Anthropic is a competitor to OpenAI, known for developing large language models for various applications.

Google announced that its Gemini desktop app for macOS can now control native Mac applications and browse the web on a user’s behalf.
The feature, called computer use, lets the AI perform multi‑step tasks after a user gives a command.
It is being rolled out in English to U.S. users who have a Gemini app and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription.
The computer‑use capability shows a live preview window in the chat so users can watch the agent act while their screen and cursor remain free for other work.
Users can pause, stop, or approve each action before it occurs, giving them control over the process.
Google says the feature can help with repetitive workflows such as filling out forms, organizing files into folders, creating slideshows from dashboards, and listing items for sale.
Access is limited to apps the user explicitly permits, and the rollout currently targets English‑speaking users in the United States.
